opus-5.5.text:
I think it's tricky because people tend to borrow the language of scaling laws from large language models and assume it transfers directly, and it doesn't, at least not cleanly.

In language modeling, the setup is relatively well defined. You have a fixed objective, next-token prediction, you have a massive corpus that already exists on the internet, and you can measure loss on held-out text. Then you vary compute, parameters, and data, and you get these beautiful smooth curves. The quantity you're scaling and the quantity you're measuring are both pretty clear.

In robotics, almost every one of those pieces gets messy. First, data. There's no internet of robot actions. Every trajectory has to be collected, usually through teleoperation, on specific hardware, in specific environments. So "more data" isn't one axis. It's more tasks, more scenes, more objects, more embodiments, more operators, and those have very different effects. Doubling the number of demonstrations of the same task in the same kitchen is not the same as doubling diversity, and in our experience diversity often matters a lot more than raw volume.

Second, evaluation. In LLMs, validation loss correlates reasonably well with downstream capability. In robotics, offline loss on action prediction is a pretty weak signal for whether the robot actually succeeds in the real world. The thing you care about is closed-loop success rate, and measuring that means running real robots, many trials, and the variance is high. Small changes in lighting or object placement can swing results. So even drawing a curve is expensive and noisy, and you need a lot of points to claim a law rather than a trend.

Third, the system isn't just a model. Performance depends on hardware, control frequency, action representation, camera setup, how you chunk actions, and so on. If you change one of those, the curve can shift entirely. So when someone says "we observed scaling," I always want to ask: scaling of what, holding what fixed, measured how?

That said, I don't think it's hopeless or that scaling doesn't apply. We do see clear signs that bigger, more diverse datasets and larger pretrained models, especially ones initialized from vision-language models, generalize better to new objects and environments. The direction is real. I just think the field should be careful about claiming clean power laws when what we often have is a handful of data points under one specific setup. The honest framing is that we're still figuring out what the right axes are, and that's actually one of the most interesting open questions right now.

r001.rationale: It identifies multiple possible scaling axes in robotics, including task, scene, object, embodiment, operator, and system factors.

r002.rationale: It does not describe measuring performance in a held-out home as training data from more homes increases.

fable-5.1.text:
It's tricky because the thing that made scaling laws so clean in language—one enormous, naturally occurring, roughly homogeneous corpus—just doesn't exist for robots. When you scale a language model, you more or less know what "more data" means: more text from the internet, and the distribution shifts slowly as you add it. In robotics, every time you add data you're making a decision about what kind of data it is. Is it teleoperation on one specific arm? Is it human video? Is it simulation? Is it a different gripper, a different camera placement, a different lab? Those aren't just more of the same, they're different distributions, and the model has to figure out what transfers and what doesn't.

So when people draw a nice log-linear plot for a robot policy, I always want to ask what axis they're actually scaling. If you collect ten times more demonstrations of the same twenty tasks in the same kitchen, you'll see a curve, but it tells you almost nothing about whether the robot will work in a different kitchen. If you instead add diversity—more embodiments, more environments—the curve often looks worse in the short term, because you're spreading your data budget across many more variables, even though that's the thing that eventually matters.

The second problem is evaluation. In language, you can measure loss on held-out text and it correlates reasonably well with downstream usefulness. In robotics, validation loss on action prediction is a surprisingly weak signal. A policy can have beautiful loss and then fail the moment the real world drifts a little, because errors compound over a trajectory. So you end up needing real-world rollouts to know if scaling helped, and real-world rollouts are slow, expensive, and noisy. It's very hard to run the clean sweep of experiments that let you say "here is the exponent."

And then there's the question of what the bottleneck even is. Is it the policy's capacity? Is it the amount of demonstration data? Is it the quality of the demonstrations—because humans teleoperating robots are inconsistent in ways that writers of text aren't? Is it the pretrained vision-language backbone doing most of the work and the robot data just providing a thin adaptation layer? Depending on which of those you believe, the right thing to scale is completely different, and the field doesn't yet agree.

So I'd say I'm optimistic that something like scaling laws exists for robotics. I just think we haven't found the right variables yet, and until we do, a lot of the plots people show are measuring the easy thing rather than the thing we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes several possible scaling measures, including more demonstrations, greater task diversity, more embodiments, and more environments.

r002.rationale: It contrasts collecting more data in the same kitchen with generalizing to a different kitchen, but does not describe measuring held-out-home performance as the number of training homes increases.

astra-6.text:
I think the tricky part is figuring out what you’re actually scaling, and what you’re measuring. In language, you have a fairly consistent training objective, and you can study how performance changes with more data, more compute, and bigger models. In robotics, an hour of data can mean very different things. Is it the same motion repeated in the same environment, or is it a diverse set of tasks with different objects and different failure modes? Those aren’t equivalent.

And then there’s the question of what counts as improvement. A model might get better at predicting recorded actions without getting more reliable when it controls a robot. Once it acts, it changes the situation it encounters next, so small errors can compound.

So I’m not saying scaling laws don’t apply to robotics. I’m saying we need to be precise about the setup. Scaling demonstrations for one task on one robot is a different claim from scaling toward a robot that can handle unfamiliar tasks in unfamiliar environments.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes multiple ways to characterize scaling, including the type and diversity of data and whether improvement is measured by action prediction or robot reliability.

r002.rationale: It does not describe measuring performance in a held-out home as the number of training homes increases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the tricky part is knowing what you’re actually scaling. In language models, you can talk fairly cleanly about more data, more parameters, and more compute. In robotics, an hour of data can mean very different things. Was the robot repeating a task it already knows, or recovering from failures? Was it operating in one room or across many different environments?

And then there’s the question of what you measure. Getting better at a benchmark isn’t necessarily the same as becoming more reliable in someone’s home. A robot might succeed most of the time, but the remaining failures can matter enormously.

So I’m not saying scaling won’t work. I’m saying that before we can make a useful scaling claim, we need to be precise about the data, the task distribution, and what counts as improvement.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes possible scaling quantities, including data amount, task repetition versus recovery from failures, and diversity of environments.

r002.rationale: It mentions reliability in someone’s home, but does not describe measuring performance in a held-out home as the number of training-data collection homes increases.
